title: Neurons
content_html:
Neurons

Do neurons operate in binary states?

At first glance neurons might appear binary because of the all-or-none principle of action potentials. When a neuron fires, it generates an action potential: a rapid spike in voltage along the axon. These spikes are all-or-none: if the input exceeds a threshold, the neuron fires a full spike; if not, nothing happens. In this sense, a single spike is binary-there is either a spike (something like “1”) or not (“0”).

But the nervous system isn’t just binary. Neurons communicate through much richer dynamics than on/off switching. Information is often carried in the frequency of spikes, not just their presence. (e.g., faster firing = stronger signal). The precise timing between spikes (millisecond differences) carries meaning. Large groups of neurons work together, with patterns of activation encoding information. Neurons also integrate smaller, graded inputs (excitatory and inhibitory postsynaptic potentials) that don’t reach firing threshold but still shape computation. Neurotransmitter types and modulators add complexity-neurons are not uniform logic gates. A neuron is an analog-digital hybrid: inputs are analog (graded voltages), the spike output is binary-like, and the network encodes information in patterns across many neurons.

Brains aren’t like digital computers, though some neural aspects can be approximated digitally. Neural computation uses parallelism, plasticity, and probabilistic coding, which makes them very different from binary switches in machines.

Connectivity

Neurons are astonishingly interconnected, though the pattern of connectivity is highly structured rather than random. The human brain has ~86 billion neurons, and each neuron makes on average ~1,000 to 10,000 synaptic connections, depending on type and location. That gives on the order of 10^14–10^15 synapses in the human brain - a scale comparable to the number of stars in the Milky Way.

In cortex, pyramidal neurons form dense local networks, with connection probabilities of 10–30% between nearby cells. Axons can extend millimeters to centimeters, linking different brain regions (e.g., corpus callosum connecting hemispheres). Some neurons act as “hubs” with disproportionately many connections (hub-and-spoke network). So the brain is structured, but not uniform; connectivity follows small-world network and scale-free principles such as high local clustering (modules specialized for tasks), and short average path length across the whole network (efficient global communication).

The brain minimizes wiring cost: axons and dendrites take paths that reduce length and metabolic expense, which leads to trade-offs: highly efficient, but not globally optimal (evolutionary tinkering again). Because neurons are massively interconnected, memory is distributed: a single memory engram is spread across many cells. Redundancy and overlapping connections make the system robust but fuzzy - contributing to the probabilistic and reconstructive aspects of memory.

Mechanism

A neuron is the fundamental unit of the brain, a specialized cell that processes and transmits information in the nervous system. It has three main parts: dendrites (tree-like branches that receive inputs), cell body which integrates signals, and axon, a single long projection that sends outputs.

Dendrites are input receivers, covered with thousands of tiny protrusions (dendritic spines). Each spine receives input from another neuron’s axon terminal. They contain receptors for neurotransmitters and can grow/shrink depending on experience (plasticity). Dendrites are the “antennas” of the neuron.

The Axon is the output pathway, a thin fiber (sometimes up to a meter long in humans) that conducts electrical impulses (action potentials) away from the soma. Branches at the end form connections with other neurons. The axon is the “cable” transmitting the message.

The synapse is the connection point where an axon terminal of one neuron communicates with a dendrite (or soma/axon) of another. Communication is usually chemical: An action potential arrives at the axon terminal, neurotransmitters are released into the synaptic cleft, which bind to receptors on the dendrite’s spine, changing its electrical state. Some synapses are excitatory (make the next neuron more likely to fire), others inhibitory. The synapse is like a “plug socket” where the signal jumps from one wire to another - but using chemicals instead of metal.

A single neuron receives thousands of synaptic inputs from different axons on its dendrites. If the summed input crosses a threshold then a spike travels down the axon to activate synapses on other neurons. The cycle repeats across billions of neurons, forming the brain’s circuits.

Probabilistic brain

The brain is probabilistic at multiple levels, from the physics of single neurons up to network dynamics and behavior. Even if you give a neuron the same input current repeatedly, it won’t always fire spikes at exactly the same time. Ion channel opening and closing is stochastic, introducing jitter in spike timing. When an action potential arrives at a synapse, neurotransmitter release happens with a probability less than 1 (often ~0.1–0.5). Sometimes vesicles release, sometimes not. At the microscale, neurons are noisy devices.

At the representational level, brains compute with probability distributions, not single values. Instead of a single “yes/no” neuron, groups of neurons encode probabilities. For example, direction-selective cells in visual cortex collectively represent the probability distribution of a stimulus direction. Many cognitive models suggest the brain performs Bayesian inference, combining prior expectations with uncertain sensory evidence to generate probabilistic beliefs. Prediction error signals (e.g., dopamine neurons) match well with probabilistic learning frameworks (reinforcement learning, prediction under uncertainty).

Attractor networks (used for memory) can fall into one of several possible stable states depending on noise and initial conditions. Oscillations and synchrony fluctuate, leading to variable integration of inputs, and plasticity rules (like spike-timing-dependent plasticity) themselves depend on probabilistic spiking, so learning is stochastic. At the systems level, outcomes emerge probabilistically from many interacting parts.

Probabilistic coding makes the system resistant to noise - individual synapse failures don’t destroy the signal. The brain can generalize, interpolate, and imagine possibilities, not just exact outcomes. By representing uncertainty, the brain can make decisions that hedge against risk (e.g., sensory illusions show how perception balances likelihoods). So, the brain is probabilistic both because of biological noise (channels, synapses) and because evolution has harnessed probability as a coding and computation strategy. Instead of deterministic “1s and 0s,” neurons collectively represent likelihoods and confidence levels.

A programming language for neurons

Neurons don’t have a formal programming language, but many neuroscientists argue that the brain does use coding “languages” - not symbolic like human code, but biological codes for representing and transforming information. Neuronal “syntax” involves action potentials (spikes). Spikes are uniform in shape, like a fixed instruction word in assembly language. What varies is when and how often spikes occur. So, the syntax of the brain’s “language” is spike timing and frequency.

The meaning of spike patterns is given by neural coding schemes, which you could think of as the semantics of the brain’s language. The way neurons connect (excitatory, inhibitory, recurrent) defines the rules of composition - like grammar in a programming language. Circuit motifs (e.g., feedforward, feedback, oscillatory loops) are reusable “control structures” (like if, while, for).

  • Synaptic weights are like compiled code: they set how signals are transformed.
  • Plasticity (learning) is like runtime editing: the “program” updates as experience changes connections.
  • Neuromodulators (dopamine, serotonin) act like “context flags” or global variables that alter how rules are applied.

Unlike formal programming languages, the brain’s “language” is probabilistic and noisy, not deterministic. It is massively parallel and distributed; there is no central “interpreter.” Evolution, not design, “wrote” the system, so it’s not tidy or optimized like human code. So, if neurons had an equivalent of a programming language, it would be a “spike code language”: a probabilistic, time-sensitive, massively parallel code where spikes are the symbols, networks provide the grammar, and meaning emerges from distributed activity.

Evolution

Human code optimization is to minimize redundancy, maximize clarity and efficiency for a specific problem. Humans can rewrite from scratch, enforce neat architecture, and target known metrics (speed, memory, readability). Evolutionary optimization maximises survival and reproduction in a changing environment. Evolution doesn’t aim for elegant code or universal efficiency - just “good enough” for survival at each step.

Neurons, circuits, and brains were built by incremental tweaks over billions of years. Old structures were repurposed (e.g., the human cortex layered on top of older reptilian and mammalian structures). Evolution often produces overlapping mechanisms, because deleting parts can be lethal, even if inefficient. It is constrained by biochemistry, embryology, and what already exists - it cannot freely redesign from scratch.

At the biophysical level, neurons and synapses are incredibly energy-efficient and reliable. The brain runs on about 20 watts (a dim lightbulb) while outperforming supercomputers in certain tasks (e.g., pattern recognition). That’s a kind of hyper-optimization. But at the architectural level, brains look messy: multiple overlapping memory systems, redundant pathways, sometimes inefficient wiring. Evolution optimizes locally, not globally. For example, a bird wing is “optimized” to fly but evolved from reptilian forelimbs - so bones, muscles, and nerves carry evolutionary baggage.

If neurons had a programming language, it wouldn’t look clean and tidy, it would look more like a huge, ancient codebase that’s been patched for billions of years: efficient in execution, but full of odd workarounds, legacy functions, and overlapping modules. So evolution does produce extremely optimized systems - but the optimization is about survival efficiency, not neatness or clarity. The result is both powerful and messy, a kind of “spaghetti code” that works astonishingly well but defies elegant design principles as we would define them.

Architecture shapes memory

The nature of memory - selective, reconstructive, sometimes distorted - is a direct outcome of the physical neural architecture shaped by evolutionary optimization. The way we process and perceive memories is inseparable from the physical architecture and dynamics of the brain’s neural networks. Physical architecture shapes memory; the Hippocampus is critical for episodic memory; its recurrent connections support pattern separation (distinguishing similar events) and pattern completion (recalling whole memories from partial cues). The Neocortex stores long-term representations; gradual consolidation distributes memory traces across wide areas. Hebbian plasticity and spike-timing-dependent plasticity shape which connections strengthen, determining what gets remembered. The very wiring diagram (connectome) constrains what forms of memory are possible; memories aren’t “files” but emergent states of physical circuits.

Because networks are probabilistic, memories are reconstructed, not replayed exactly. This reconstruction process introduces distortion, forgetting, and blending - but also flexibility, generalization, and imagination. The “messiness” of evolution (redundancy, overlapping systems) means memory is robust but not perfectly accurate. If memory were engineered top-down, we might expect crisp, lossless storage and retrieval. Instead, we have an evolved system that trades accuracy for adaptiveness: imperfect recall supports creativity and planning, distributed, redundant storage protects against local brain damage, and energy efficiency (~20 W brain) limits how much can be stored, so the system prioritizes relevance over completeness.

Memory storage

Even though memory is reconstructive, there has to be some kind of storage substrate in the brain. The important nuance is that what’s stored is not a perfect “recording” but dispositional traces that make reconstruction possible. The prevailing view is that memory is encoded in long-term changes in synaptic strength between neurons (Hebbian learning, long-term potentiation/depression). A given memory is not in a single place, but across networks of neurons - often called memory engrams. Dendritic spines, receptor densities, and even small-scale wiring changes (new connections) act as durable substrates. Proteins and gene-expression states within neurons also contribute to stabilizing memories.

Memories are not stored as literal snapshots. Instead, each experience leaves behind patterns of modified connections. These patterns are fragmentary - enough to bias network dynamics so that with partial cues, the whole experience can be reconstructed. Think of it like saving recipes for reactivating patterns, not video clips. When you recall, the hippocampus helps reassemble these distributed traces into a coherent event. The neocortex provides the perceptual, semantic, and contextual fragments. Attractor dynamics in recurrent circuits allow a memory to “settle” into a stable representation, even if the starting cue is incomplete.

So, here is real storage - but it’s not like saving a file. Instead, memories are stored as distributed, dynamic patterns in the physical architecture of synapses, circuits, and molecular states, which provide the scaffold for later reconstruction.

An isolated memory

The answer depends on what we mean by a “single specific memory.” Memory is distributed, not localized, so a specific memory (e.g., your 10th birthday) is not stored in one “cell” or spot. Instead, it is represented by an engram - a pattern of activity across thousands to millions of neurons. This engram is distributed across the hippocampus, neocortex, and other areas (e.g., amygdala for emotional components). In rodent studies using optogenetics, researchers have identified engrams with ~2–5% of neurons in a given hippocampal region active for one memory. In a mouse hippocampal subregion with ~100,000 neurons, that would be a few thousand cells participating in one memory trace. In humans, scaling is harder - but similar principles suggest tens of thousands to millions of neurons participate in a single episodic memory.

Because each engaged neuron connects to thousands of others (on the order of 10³–10⁴ synapses), a single memory likely involves millions to billions of synaptic modifications, though not unique to that memory - many are shared across overlapping experiences. Strengthening/weakening of subsets of synapses encodes the memory trace.

Many neurons/synapses are altered by learning, creating the engram. A smaller subset of cue-triggered neurons can reactivate the whole pattern (pattern completion). So, recall might begin with hundreds or thousands of neurons, but rapidly spreads to recruit the full distributed network. A specific episodic memory probably involves ~10⁴–10⁶ neurons (depending on scale and complexity), ~10⁷–10⁹ (hundreds of millions) synapses participating in altered weights. These numbers are highly approximate, but they reflect the scale of distributed storage across multiple brain regions.

Quantum brain

In The Emperor’s New Mind (1989) and Shadows of the Mind (1994), Roger Penrose argued that consciousness cannot be explained by classical computation alone. He suggested instead that quantum processes inside neurons might play a role in consciousness, enabling non-computable influences on brain activity. Microtubules - structural proteins inside neurons - were proposed as the substrate for quantum computation, whereby neural processes “orchestrate” quantum states in microtubules. Penrose hypothesized a new type of wavefunction collapse tied to quantum gravity, providing a “non-computable” element. The idea was that consciousness arises from cycles of quantum superposition and collapse inside microtubules, amplified to influence neural firing.

Many physicists argued that quantum states in warm, wet neurons would decohere in femtoseconds - far too fast to play a functional role in cognition. To date, there’s no direct evidence that microtubules sustain long-lived quantum states relevant to neural computation. Neuroscience explains most memory, learning, and perception without needing quantum computation. The theory remains highly controversial, but it has kept alive the discussion of whether quantum mechanics might have a role in brain function.
